Chapter 4

Tangent Spaces

Motivation: Vectors without arrows

In \(\mathbb{R}^d\), a vector \(v\) at \(p\) is an arrow from \(p\) to \(p + v\). On a manifold this picture is unavailable, since points cannot be added and there is no ambient space for the arrows to live in. What survives is the action of \(v\) on functions. In \(\mathbb{R}^d\), along the curve \(\gamma(\lambda) = p + \lambda v\), \[ (f \circ \gamma)'(0) = v^i \, \partial_i f(p) , \] and choosing for \(f\) the coordinate functions recovers every component \(v^i\). Curves and smooth functions both make sense on a manifold, so this action can serve as the definition of a vector.

Goal. Build, at every point \(p \in \mathcal{M}\), the vector spaces of Chapter 2.

  • Define the tangent space \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) as the set of velocities of curves through \(p\), acting on scalar fields as directional derivatives, and show that it is a \(d\)-dimensional vector space.

  • Derive, rather than postulate, the chart-induced bases and the transformation laws of components, which distinguish covariant from contravariant objects.

  • Construct its dual, the cotangent space \(T^*_p\mathcal{M}\), whose elements are the differentials of scalar fields, and the tensor spaces \(T^{(r,s)}_p\mathcal{M}\).

The four-velocity of a particle is the velocity of its worldline at a point of spacetime, an element of \(T_p\mathcal{M}\).
